purpose: The Training Zone: every corner type, phase by phase, taught the way the live coaching sessions worked — FEELING first (the words a driver actually says), then a PICTURE of what the car is physically doing, then the tune rack showing which of the nine tabs own it, then the RATIO PAIRS at both extremes, then the options ladder. Built on the grip-slide spectrum so dirt racing (where grip and drift technique blend) slots in as a first-class citizen.

ratio_doctrine.headline: Almost every tuning tab is a FRONT : REAR pair — and a single number means nothing until you know its partner.
ratio_doctrine.principle: The RATIO between the pair decides BALANCE: which end of the car runs out of grip first. The MAGNITUDE of the pair decides CHARACTER: how sharp or how forgiving the car is when it gets there. This is why '45 rear anti-roll bar' is not a setting — it is half of a setting. Change one side of a pair and you changed the balance; change both sides together and you changed the character while keeping the balance.

pairs.ratio: which end breaks away first (higher pressure = smaller patch = lets go sooner)
pairs.magnitude: overall grip and how fast the tires reach temperature

pairs.ratio: where each corner's exit lands in the powerband
which end keeps its contact patch flat under lean
pairs.magnitude: sustained-load grip bought at the cost of straight-line braking

pairs.ratio: turn-in eagerness vs rear straight-line calm
pairs.magnitude: stability bought at the cost of tire scrub and top speed

pairs.ratio: THE balance dial — your stiffer end loses grip first
pairs.magnitude: how quickly the car takes its set in a corner
compliance over bumps vs body control

pairs.ratio: static weight bias and aero platform angle
pairs.magnitude: centre-of-gravity height — lower is better until it bottoms out

pairs.ratio: how fast load LEAVES an end vs how fast it ARRIVES
pairs.magnitude: transient violence — the whip lives here

pairs.ratio: which end settles first after an input
high-speed balance (the panel's Aero Balance number)
pairs.magnitude: total grip at speed, paid for in drag and top speed

pairs.ratio: which end locks, and whether the rear keeps grip for cornering

pairs.magnitude: how tied-together that axle's wheels are

pairs.ratio: where drive goes — and therefore how much steering the front tires can spare
pairs.magnitude: traction off the line vs rotation in the corner

ratio_doctrine.reading_rule: When a car misbehaves, do not ask 'what should this slider be?' Ask 'which pair owns this phase, and is my ratio pointing the wrong way?' Then move ONE side of ONE pair.

spectrum.concept: Grip driving and drifting are not different pages — they are ends of one spectrum, and the position on it is set by SURFACE and INTENT. On tarmac, peak traction is at tiny slip angles: slides are slow, so tuning fights rotation. On LOOSE surfaces, peak traction physically occurs AT significant slip — the tire bites by cutting into the surface — so controlled sliding IS the fast line, and dirt tuning borrows drift sliders at half strength. Full drift maximises angle and abandons lap time entirely.

stations.label: Tarmac race
stations.doctrine: Rotation is the enemy past the apex. Sliders damp it and catch it.

stations.label: Dirt / rally race
stations.doctrine: THE BRIDGE: slide to set the angle BEFORE the apex, exit straight. Drift diff philosophy (high accel lock) + grip braking + soft rally suspension. Rotation is a tool with a budget.
stations.status: seeded — full dirt chapter is the next build

stations.label: Drift
stations.doctrine: Angle is the product. Every slider cultivates rotation and then CATCHES it (caster 7.0, toe-out, soft-front/stiff-rear bars, diff locked).

conditions.headline: Before you blame a slider — the conditions layer. These modify EVERYTHING below; every one was learned the hard way in a live session.

checks.feeling: "Any little steer and the tires give out all grip."
checks.mechanism: Tires below operating temperature grip at a fraction of their rating — and compounds differ wildly: slicks are the most cold-sensitive rubber in the game, rally barely cares. Rivals restarts reset tire temperature, so the first ~2 minutes after every restart tests cold rubber, not your tune.
checks.tells: Every incident happens in the first 20-30s of a run; the same corner is fine mid-session; the car got WORSE right after you upgraded to a grippier compound.
checks.options: Warm 2-3 min before judging anything (weaving and hard braking heat faster) · lower pressures reach temperature sooner · the telemetry Tires page shows live temps · rally compound if restart-loop testing matters more than peak grip.
checks.tier: player-verified (fork B: four consecutive cold-start crashes, zero warm ones)

checks.feeling: "At slow speed it's twitchy, but at high speed the ability to turn goes completely out the window."
checks.mechanism: You are driving TWO cars: the mechanical car (springs, bars, weight — owns low speed) and the aero car (downforce grows with speed squared — owns 80mph+). When Mech. Balance and Aero Balance differ, the car's personality morphs as speed rises.
checks.tells: Compare the panel's Mech. Balance against Aero Balance — the GAP is the morph. A gap of 0.06 is one consistent car; 0.20 is two different cars.
checks.options: Close the gap from the AERO side to fix the fast end without disturbing the slow end · slow-corner complaints belong to mechanical sliders, fast-corner complaints to aero. Never fix a hairpin with a wing.

checks.feeling: "The balance is right but it STILL pushes / still won't hold the corner."
checks.mechanism: Sliders distribute grip; the COMPOUND sets the total. When balance tuning stops paying, you have hit the tire's ceiling — the envelope is maxed and only parts move it.
checks.tells: Both ends give up together; the same corner fails at the same speed regardless of balance; the lateral-G readouts stop responding to slider changes.
checks.options: Tire width (parts, PI) · compound upgrade (big PI — rebudgets the whole build) · accept the corner's entry-speed number · momentum lines instead of V-lines.
checks.tier: player-verified (4C fork A: balance solved to a 0.08 gap, push remained — the compound was the wall)

checks.feeling: "On dirt the grip car plows, and the drifty guys are somehow faster."
checks.mechanism: Loose surfaces move peak traction to LARGE slip angles — the tire grips by digging, not sticking. The fast dirt line carries rotation that the tarmac line would call a mistake.
checks.tells: Tidy tarmac technique feels slow; small slides self-correct instead of growing; the car rewards an early flick.
checks.options: Rally compound + soft rally springs · diff accel HIGH (drift philosophy at half strength) · slide before the apex, straight after it · see the Dirt corner archetype below.
checks.tier: doctrine (dirt chapter seeded — full build next)

corner_types.name: Hairpin
corner_types.regime: 100% MECHANICAL — the wing is asleep; tires, springs, bars and diff do everything

entries.feeling: "The back slides out when I'm braking and turning."
entries.mechanism: Trail-braking stacks three systems on the rear axle at once: brake bias sitting too far rearward while weight leaves that end, the differential's decel lock dragging the driveline, and rebound letting the rear unload too fast. The rear is asked for braking AND cornering grip exactly when it has the least of both.

visual.caption: Rear steps out under trail braking — nose points well inside the direction of travel, countersteer already applied

ratios.lo_feel: the rear does the stopping, locks early and swings the moment you add steering
ratios.hi_feel: the nose does the stopping; the rear keeps grip in reserve for cornering
ratios.why: the matrix's PRIMARY fix for entry oversteer — move work off the axle that is already starving

ratios.lo_feel: lifting rotates the car instantly — great for drift, terrifying under brakes
ratios.hi_feel: the rear wheels stay tied together off-throttle; lift-off oversteer calms down
ratios.why: the game's own description: raising rear Decel 'can reduce lift off oversteer'

ratios.lo_feel: the rear rises lazily as the nose dives — but too soft and it floats
ratios.hi_feel: the rear is yanked up fast under the dive and goes light — the classic snap
ratios.why: rebound controls how fast load LEAVES the rear; too stiff and it unloads itself

entries.options: Technique first: finish more of the braking BEFORE turn-in. Then brake balance, then rear decel, one per test drive.
entries.tier: player-verified (the fix that tamed both the 4C and the Viper replica)
telemetry: Friction — rear circles redline first while the fronts stay green
Body Acceleration — the dot sits on the braking edge, then swings sideways as you steer
Suspension — front corners compressed, rear extended (the dive that unloads the rear)

entries.feeling: "It just refuses to turn at low speed — I have to slow way below the corner to make it."
entries.mechanism: Below roughly 60 mph there is NO aero help — mechanical front grip is all that exists, and a heavy or powerful build usually has less of it than the corner is asking for. The wheels are turned; the car simply travels on.

visual.caption: Wheels cranked, body barely rotating — the front tires are sliding and the car runs to the outside

ratios.lo_feel: the nose bites and the rear rotates around it — lively, can snap
ratios.hi_feel: the front lets go first and plows straight on — safe and slow
ratios.why: your STIFFER end loses grip first; a pushing car wants the softer front of the pair

ratios.lo_feel: bigger front patch — more bite, slower response
ratios.hi_feel: smaller front patch — sharper initial turn, less ultimate grip
ratios.why: at hairpin speeds patch size beats response; drop the front toward the band's floor

ratios.lo_feel: the nose loads up and digs in on turn-in
ratios.hi_feel: the nose stays flat, transfers less load onto the front tires, pushes
ratios.why: same balance logic as the bars, with a compliance cost

entries.options: Parts beat sliders here: front tire WIDTH is the honest fix. Line: a V-line (deep brake, rotate, point and shoot) beats trying to carry speed.
entries.tier: player-verified (Viper assessment: the ACR's one structural weakness)
telemetry: Friction — FRONT circles go red while the rears stay green (the mirror image of entry oversteer)
Heat — front outer edges hottest = the patch is rolling over, not gripping

entries.feeling: "Any throttle and the tires spin — and on AWD the steering disappears at the same time."
entries.mechanism: Torque overwhelms slow-corner grip. THE AWD INSIGHT: the centre differential sends power to the FRONT tires too — and a spinning tire has almost no lateral grip, so your steering evaporates the instant you stomp. One cause, two sensations.

visual.caption: All four spinning under power — steering input present, nothing happening; the car drives straight off the exit

ratios.lo_feel: the front tires are steering AND driving — they do neither well
ratios.hi_feel: the fronts are freed to steer; the rear takes the torque hit
ratios.why: the direct fix for AWD steering-evaporation on exit

ratios.lo_feel: the fronts pull evenly and keep steering
ratios.hi_feel: the fronts lock together and drag the nose wide under power
ratios.why: less front lock = less push while accelerating

ratios.lo_feel: explosive off the line, overwhelms the tires out of slow corners
ratios.hi_feel: torque arrives softer in every gear — the automatic's friend
ratios.why: player-verified: 0-60 IMPROVED (2.63 → 2.43) with TALLER gearing because the wheelspin was eating the launch

entries.options: Automatic players: SQUEEZE the throttle — a stomp commands a kickdown, and the downshift IS the torque dump. Taller final drive is how you 'short-shift' when you cannot hold a gear.
telemetry: Tires, Misc. — driven wheels read much higher SPEED than the others: wheelspin, measured
General — throttle % against the gear the auto picked (the kickdown, caught in the act)

corner_types.name: High-speed sweeper
corner_types.regime: AERO — downforce is most of the grip; the mechanical car is a passenger

entries.feeling: "If I add even a little steering while braking, the whole thing lets go."
entries.mechanism: Braking from high speed transfers huge load forward while the rear's aero load is simultaneously bleeding away with speed. Steering on top of that asks a light, unloaded rear to corner. Three invisible systems stack in this half-second: brake bias, decel lock, rebound.

visual.caption: Big slip angle developing under braking at speed — the rear has neither weight nor downforce left

ratios.lo_feel: the rear locks under load transfer and the car pivots
ratios.hi_feel: stable, straight stops — the rear keeps grip for the steering you are about to add
ratios.why: same #1 fix as the hairpin, at far higher stakes

ratios.lo_feel: planted rear, pushy nose — safe entries, lazy corners
ratios.hi_feel: eager nose, light rear — fast corners, knife-edge entries
ratios.why: NEVER trim rear wing while entry is unstable — rear downforce IS the entry safety net

ratios.lo_feel: every lift rotates the car
ratios.hi_feel: the rear stays tied together through the brake-release moment
ratios.why: stabilises the exact instant where the crashes happen

entries.options: Brake in a straight line, then commit. Every corner has an entry-speed number (v = √(g · radius · latG)) — find it once and respect it.
entries.tier: player-verified (video forensics: every filmed crash began in this half-second)
telemetry: Body Acceleration — watch the dot leave the braking edge and cross the circle boundary as steering is added
Friction — the rear pair spikes past 100% first

entries.feeling: "High-speed corners just aren't wide enough — it washes to the outside no matter what I do."
entries.mechanism: The front's share of aero is too small: as speed rises the grip mix slides rearward and the front axle saturates first. Or you are simply above the envelope — beyond the speed the total grip can support at that radius.

visual.caption: Body nearly aligned with travel, front tires saturated — a long, helpless drift to the outside kerb

ratios.lo_feel: the faster you go, the more it understeers
ratios.hi_feel: the nose keeps biting at speed; the rear becomes the limiting end
ratios.why: the game's description: 'the lower your Balance value, the more understeer'

ratios.lo_feel: the loaded outside tire rolls onto its shoulder and gives up
ratios.hi_feel: the outside tire stands flat under lean — the high-speed front-grip slider
ratios.why: camber pays in SUSTAINED load — exactly this corner, and almost nothing in hairpins

entries.options: DIAGNOSTIC GOLD: watch the skill popups. A DRIFT skill firing means the REAR broke away (opposite problem, opposite fix). No skill and just wide = front push, this row.
telemetry: Friction — front Peak % climbing while the rears stay comfortable
Body Acceleration — lateral G plateaus and refuses to rise: you are at the envelope, not at a balance problem

entries.feeling: "The rear lights up mid-corner when I feed throttle at 100+."
entries.mechanism: Sustained lateral G is already spending most of the rear tires' grip budget; supercharger or turbo torque at high rpm takes the rest. The slide starts driven, then momentum carries it wide.

visual.caption: Power-on rear breakaway in the aero regime — the slide begins driven, then momentum takes over

ratios.lo_feel: the rear lights progressively, one wheel at a time — recoverable
ratios.hi_feel: both rear wheels break as one locked axle — sudden and total
ratios.why: lower accel lock buys progressive breakaway when grip is already spent

ratios.lo_feel: exit throttle you can trust, at the cost of straight-line speed
ratios.hi_feel: big top speed, and a rear that runs out mid-corner
ratios.why: on a flowing course this is the real trade: 11 mph of top end bought 0.09g and shorter braking

entries.options: Throttle discipline: wait for the corner to open before committing. On an automatic, squeeze — the kickdown is the enemy.
telemetry: Tires, Misc. — rear wheel speeds jump above the fronts at the moment of throttle
Friction — rear circles red, fronts green

corner_types.name: Chicane / direction changes
corner_types.regime: TRANSIENT — the invisible layer's home: damping, toe and bars own everything here

entries.feeling: "It whips left and right — almost uncontrollably."
entries.mechanism: Each direction change swings the car's mass across the chassis. If rebound cannot control how fast the unloading side springs back, every swap adds energy instead of absorbing it and the oscillation GROWS. Stiff rear bars and lift-off decel shove add to the pile.

visual.caption: Yaw oscillation: the rear overshoots one way, the correction overshoots the other — each swap bigger than the last

ratios.lo_feel: the car is a pendulum — every input keeps ringing
ratios.hi_feel: one swap, one settle — the whip dies
ratios.why: THE owner of the whip; stiff springs without matching rebound guarantee oscillation

ratios.lo_feel: the rear swings freely into every transition
ratios.hi_feel: the rear tires resist the flick geometrically — cheap stability
ratios.why: the textbook anti-whip alignment setting

ratios.lo_feel: rotation on demand, and rotation you did not ask for
ratios.hi_feel: calmer, safer transitions at the cost of agility
ratios.why: a stiff-rear split on a light car is an oscillation amplifier

entries.options: If the whip survives every slider, it is the BUILD (escalation rule): the car may be too light and short for its power, or it needs adjustable dampers it does not have.
telemetry: Suspension — the offsets swing left-right and do NOT settle between inputs: oscillation, visible
Body Acceleration — the dot ping-pongs across the circle instead of tracing an arc

entries.feeling: "It's slow and ponderous through the flick — it never settles for the second apex."
entries.mechanism: The opposite disease: too soft everywhere, so the weight is still sloshing from the first input when the second one arrives.

visual.caption: Lazy transition — the body is still rolling from the first input as the second arrives

ratios.lo_feel: forgiving, floaty, slow to change direction
ratios.hi_feel: immediate response, punishing over kerbs and bumps
ratios.why: raise BOTH sides to change character without touching balance — the magnitude rule in action

ratios.lo_feel: wallowy, delayed
ratios.hi_feel: crisp, and one notch too far becomes the whip above
ratios.why: crisp and whippy are the same line viewed from opposite sides

entries.options: One notch at a time — the gap between crisp and whippy is thin, and it is the same gap.
telemetry: Suspension — offsets change slowly and lag your inputs: the car is still rolling when the next corner arrives

corner_types.name: Flat-out kink
corner_types.regime: COMMITMENT — one binary question: does it stay flat?

entries.feeling: "Do I lift or is it flat? It wiggled last lap and now I don't trust it."
entries.mechanism: A kink at this speed is pure aero and stability. If the rear is aero-light — wing trimmed, balance too far forward — the car is riding exactly at its stability margin, and a bump or a lift AT the kink transfers just enough load to snap it.

visual.caption: Everything at the limit but nothing broken — the margin is thin enough that a bump or a lift decides it

ratios.lo_feel: planted and trustworthy flat out; slower everywhere else
ratios.hi_feel: sharp turn-in at speed; the rear becomes a question you ask every lap
ratios.why: rear downforce is the stability budget — spend it last, after everything else is proven

ratios.lo_feel: free, floaty at high speed
ratios.hi_feel: the rear tracks straight — cheap high-speed insurance
ratios.why: tiny cost, large confidence return on a fast course

entries.options: If you must lift, lift BEFORE the kink, never in it. The panel's lateral G at 120 is this corner's rating — compare it against what the kink demands.
entries.tier: player-verified (the wing-trim gate: rear-stability evidence required before trimming)
telemetry: Body Acceleration — the dot riding the ring edge at high speed with no margin left
Friction — all four near their peaks simultaneously

entries.feeling: "At high speed I can wiggle the wheel and it feels like it's about to spin — other cars just deafen the wiggles."
entries.mechanism: This is YAW DAMPING, not a slide. A small wiggle yaws the car; the rear tires build slip angle and — because the rear axle sits behind the centre of gravity — generate a STRAIGHTENING moment. A stable car's restoring force beats the disturbance and the wobble dies. An unstable one leaves residual yaw behind after each input, so the next wiggle starts from a worse place and the oscillation grows. Polar moment of inertia decides the baseline: mass centralised (mid-engine, short wheelbase) starts AND stops rotating easily — agile and nervous; mass spread with a long wheelbase resists both — the 'deafening' feel.

visual.caption: Yaw oscillation at speed: each correction leaves residual rotation, and the next input starts from a worse place

ratios.lo_feel: every small input yaws the car and nothing pushes back
ratios.hi_feel: the rear geometrically resists yaw — wiggles die on their own
ratios.why: THE anti-wiggle setting: nearly free, purely geometric, works at every speed

ratios.lo_feel: the car rings like a bell after each input
ratios.hi_feel: one input, one settle — the oscillation decays
ratios.why: rebound IS the decay rate of the oscillation

ratios.lo_feel: stability that GROWS with speed — exactly where you need it
ratios.hi_feel: top speed, and a car that gets looser the faster it goes
ratios.why: rear downforce is the only stabiliser that scales with speed² — trimming it is how you buy this symptom

ratios.lo_feel: more rear grip = more restoring force
ratios.hi_feel: rear lets go first = the wiggle turns into a slide
ratios.why: same balance dial, judged by stability rather than rotation

entries.options: Chassis sets the baseline and you cannot tune it away: low mass + centralised weight + short wheelbase (mid-engine) will always be nervous; long, front-heavy cars self-damp. Read Front % and weight before blaming the tune. If the car must stay nervous, drive it with smaller inputs and let the wheel self-centre rather than steering it back.
telemetry: Suspension — corner offsets swinging left-right and never settling between inputs: the oscillation, measured
Body Acceleration — the dot ping-pongs across the circle instead of tracing a clean arc
Friction — rear Peak % spiking with each wiggle while the fronts stay calm: the rear is doing all the correcting
entries.tier: player-verified (the 4C whip vs the Viper's stability — the same phenomenon at both extremes)

corner_types.name: Dirt corner (the bridge)
corner_types.regime: GRIP-SLIDE HYBRID — peak traction lives AT slip on loose surfaces; rotation is a tool with a budget
corner_types.status: SEEDED — the full dirt chapter extends from here (next build)

entries.feeling: "The grip car just plows on dirt — and the drifty guys are somehow faster."
entries.mechanism: On a loose surface the tire grips by DIGGING: peak traction is at 10-25° of slip, not 5°. The fast line rotates the car BEFORE the apex — lift, flick or brake-slide — so the exit is already straight while tarmac technique is still mid-turn.

visual.caption: Controlled rotation set EARLY — all four tires sliding on purpose, angle established before the apex

ratios.lo_feel: the car resists rotation — it plows and the slide never sets
ratios.hi_feel: lift rotates it, throttle sustains it: the dirt technique works
ratios.why: dirt borrows the drift diff at roughly half strength — rotation is a tool here, not a fault

ratios.lo_feel: the tires follow the surface and keep digging — compliance IS grip on dirt
ratios.hi_feel: the car skates across the bumps and never bites
ratios.why: on loose surfaces compliance beats body control; this is the biggest single tarmac-to-dirt change

ratios.lo_feel: bigger, softer footprint that digs in
ratios.hi_feel: skittery, bouncing over the loose stuff
ratios.why: the rally reference: drop about 3 psi from the road baseline

entries.options: Technique: lift and turn early, let the car set its own angle, then use throttle to straighten it. This is drift's initiation phase grafted onto a race line.
entries.tier: doctrine (drift research verified the sliders; dirt-specific tuning = next chapter)
telemetry: Friction — all four sliding with peaks ABOVE tarmac numbers and the car still stable: proof the dirt plateau is real
Tires, Misc. — wheel speeds differ across the axle while the car tracks true

entries.feeling: "It slides too far and I spin, or I fishtail down the whole straight."
entries.mechanism: The rotation budget overdrew: the slide outlived the corner. Dirt exits reward getting STRAIGHT early — a sliding exit is a slow exit even on loose surface.

visual.caption: Over-rotation past the apex — the angle that was a tool has become a spin

ratios.lo_feel: the front pulls the car straight out of the slide — spin insurance
ratios.hi_feel: maximum rotation, maximum angle, no safety net
ratios.why: 75-90% rear is the dirt-RACE band; 90-100% is for drift scoring

ratios.lo_feel: every lift adds more angle — the fishtail feeds itself
ratios.hi_feel: lift-off rotation is budgeted, not unlimited
ratios.why: the throttle is your angle dial; decel decides how much the lift adds

ratios.lo_feel: the tail keeps hunting down the straight
ratios.hi_feel: the rear settles and tracks
ratios.why: the same anti-fishtail setting the chicane uses

entries.options: AWD at 75-90% rear is the dirt-race sweet band: enough front pull to catch the slide, enough rear bias to rotate on command.
telemetry: Friction — rear peaks running away from the fronts
Body Acceleration — the dot pinned sideways well past the point where it should have unwound

grip_science.headline: Grip is highest RIGHT BEFORE it is lost — and that is the whole game.

slip_curve.concept: A tire does not grip in proportion to how hard you ask. Grip climbs as slip angle grows, reaches a PEAK, and then FALLS. The fast driver lives at the top of that hill. Past the peak you get less grip AND more angle at the same time — which is why a slide, once started, accelerates itself.
slip_curve.why_it_feels_sudden: On tarmac the far side of the peak is a CLIFF: a couple of degrees past the top and grip collapses. That is the 'it just let go with no warning' feeling. Lower pressures, softer compounds and progressive damping do not raise the peak much — they widen it, turning the cliff into a slope you can feel coming.

surfaces.label: Slick / semi-slick (tarmac)
surfaces.note: Highest peak, sharpest cliff. Enormous grip if you can live at 7°, brutal punishment at 12°.

surfaces.label: Rally compound on tarmac
surfaces.note: Lower peak, slightly kinder fall — the PI-arbitrage trade in one line.

surfaces.label: Rally compound on dirt
surfaces.note: THE BRIDGE: peak moves far right and the top becomes a PLATEAU. The tire grips by digging, so 20° of slip is not a mistake — it is the operating point. This is why dirt rewards sliding and tarmac punishes it.

zones.label: Past the cliff on tarmac · the plateau on dirt
Drift country — angle is the product, lap time is gone

traction_circle.concept: Each tire has ONE grip budget and it is spent in every direction at once. Braking uses it, cornering uses it, accelerating uses it — and the total is a VECTOR, not a sum. Draw the budget as a circle: any combination inside the circle is fine, anything outside is a slide.
traction_circle.why_trail_braking_is_knife_edge: At 100% braking you are already ON the circle's edge. Add even a small steering input and the combined vector points OUTSIDE it — so the tire lets go, and it lets go at the end you loaded least. This is the exact mechanism behind 'if I add even a little steering while braking, the whole thing lets go'.
traction_circle.the_trade: Because it is a circle, the way to buy cornering grip is to give back braking grip. Release the brakes progressively as you add steering and the vector stays on the edge the whole way — that is trail-braking done right, and it is the fastest path through a corner entry.
traction_circle.tuning_link: Tuning cannot enlarge one tire's circle (that is compound and load) — but it decides how the four circles are FILLED. Brake balance shifts how much braking each end spends; the differential decides whether the rears spend together or separately; aero inflates all four circles at speed; camber and pressure decide how much of each circle the contact patch can actually reach.

telemetry_proof: FRICTION page = the traction circle made literal, per wheel. Each wheel shows a circle with an orange slip vector and a Peak %. Green ring = that tire is inside its friction limit; red ring = it has been exceeded. Watch which corner goes red FIRST — that is your answer, not a guess.

BODY ACCELERATION page = the whole-car traction circle: a live dot inside a ring with a numeric G-Force. The dot's distance from centre is how much of the total budget you are using; the direction is where it is being spent (down = braking, sideways = cornering, diagonal = both).
TIRES, MISC. per-wheel SPEED = a wheelspin and lock-up detector: a spinning wheel reads far higher mph than its neighbours, a locked one reads far lower.
HEAT page = where the contact patch is actually working (inner/middle/outer) — the camber ground truth.

telemetry.headline: The seven telemetry pages — what each one proves
telemetry.how: Cycle pages with Previous/Next while driving. Record 10-30 seconds of video and read it back frame by frame; the numbers move too fast to read live.

pages.name: General
pages.shows: Power, Torque, Boost, RPM, Gear, Clutch, E-brake, Steering angle, Throttle %, Brake %, Speed
pages.proves: Driver inputs vs car response — the honest record of whether you stomped or squeezed, and where the auto chose to shift.

pages.name: Body Acceleration
pages.shows: Whole-car G-force circle with a live dot + numeric G
pages.proves: How much of the total grip budget is in use and in which direction — the traction circle, live.

pages.name: Friction
pages.shows: Per-wheel friction circles, orange slip vector, Peak % per corner, ring colour green/red
pages.proves: WHICH tire exceeded its limit and by how much — the single best grip-loss diagnostic in the game.

pages.name: Tires, Misc.
pages.shows: Per-wheel temp, live pressure, wear %, individual wheel SPEED, live dynamic camber
pages.proves: Hot pressures (subtract ~3.5 psi for the cold setting), wheelspin/lock-up by wheel-speed mismatch, and what camber the tire actually runs under load.

pages.name: Heat
pages.shows: Inner / middle / outer temperature for all four tires
pages.proves: Camber correctness — target inner about 10-15°F hotter than outer; outer hottest means not enough negative camber.

pages.name: Suspension
pages.proves: Roll and pitch behaviour, bottoming out, and — watched over a chicane — whether the car is oscillating instead of settling.

pages.name: Damage

controllability.headline: Breaks away on command, comes back on command — the dual-character build
controllability.concept: Two different cars feel 'uncontrollable': the one that snaps sideways at a handbrake tap, and the one that clings until it lets go all at once. Both are failures of the SAME property — the shape of the slip curve and the size of the front's reserve. A car you can break and catch needs three separate qualities, and they are tuned by three different families.

three_qualities.name: RELEASE AUTHORITY — can I break it when I choose?
three_qualities.question: Does a handbrake tap, a lift, or a stab of throttle reliably start the rotation?
three_qualities.high: handbrake tap = instant angle; lift-off rotates on demand
three_qualities.low: the car ignores your inputs and understeers on regardless

sliders.why: a locked decel diff FIGHTS the handbrake and the lift — this is the single biggest release lever, and the reason some cars simply refuse to rotate off-throttle
your stiffer end lets go first — this is you choosing WHICH end breaks
smaller rear patch releases earlier and more predictably

sliders.dir: some rearward bias, or lower overall pressure
sliders.why: the handbrake and trail-brake both need the rear able to lock

sliders.dir: enough power to spin the rears in 2nd-3rd
sliders.why: throttle-initiation only exists if the engine can outmuscle the tire

three_qualities.name: CATCH AUTHORITY — can I get it back?
three_qualities.question: When the rear is out, does the front have enough grip and self-centering to pull the car straight?
three_qualities.high: countersteer bites instantly, the wheel wants to straighten itself, the car re-hooks cleanly
three_qualities.low: you countersteer and nothing happens — the front is sliding too, and the spin completes

sliders.why: THE catch slider — leans the steering axis back so the wheel self-centres and the car catches its own slide; also adds camber as lock grows

sliders.dir: -2 to -3 (more than a pure grip build)
sliders.why: at big countersteer angles the front tire is heavily leaned — camber keeps its patch flat exactly when you need the catch
the front must out-grip the rear during the catch; softer = more grip

sliders.dir: as much front as the build allows
sliders.why: the parts-level version of the same rule — front reserve IS catch authority
a trickle of front drive physically PULLS the car straight — the most forgiving catch mechanism in the game

three_qualities.name: PROGRESSIVITY — does it warn me before it goes?
three_qualities.question: Is the far side of the grip peak a slope you can feel, or a cliff you fall off?
three_qualities.high: the rear eases out over a car length of road; you feel it start and can meter it
three_qualities.low: everything is fine, then the car is sideways with no intermediate state

sliders.dir: toward the lower end of the band
sliders.why: lower pressure widens the peak — the same total grip, delivered with warning
stiff damping makes load arrive at the tire faster than you can react — instant transitions with no build-up
slower weight transfer = the slide develops at human speed

sliders.dir: rally/drift compounds are progressive; slicks are a cliff
sliders.why: the biggest single influence on peak SHAPE — slicks have the highest peak and the sharpest fall
very light cars transition faster than you can catch; heavy cars are progressive but need real front grip to recover

the_measurable_test.name: The breakaway-margin test (Friction telemetry page)
the_measurable_test.procedure: Provoke a slide — handbrake tap or a lift mid-corner — while the telemetry Friction page is up, and record it. Read back the frame at the moment the rear breaks.
the_measurable_test.read: You want the REAR circles red while the FRONT circles are still GREEN with visible margin. That margin IS your catch authority, measured. If all four go red together, the car cannot be caught by anyone — that is a build problem, not a skill problem.
the_measurable_test.tune_toward: Widen the gap: everything that adds front grip (softer front bar, front camber, front width, lower front pressure) or removes rear grip (stiffer rear bar, higher rear pressure) increases breakaway margin. The dual-character car is the one with the LARGEST front-to-rear friction gap that still holds grip when driven tidily.

controllability.car_side: Some of this is the chassis, not the tune: a long wheelbase rotates slowly and forgivingly; a short one snaps. Mid-engine cars swing their mass hard once past the peak (the 4C); front-engine cars hang their mass ahead of the pivot and self-stabilise (the Viper). RWD gives the cleanest release AND the cleanest catch; AWD trades some release authority for a front axle that rescues you.
controllability.tier: doctrine — assembled from the verified drift slider research (caster/camber/ARB/diff) plus the player-verified grip sessions; the breakaway-margin test is newly proposed and untested
